decisions.headline: Nasdaq 100 posts worst week since March 2020
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Stocks] Nasdaq 100 posts worst week since March 2020
Both Nasdaq indices close just above their 100-week moving averages after a broad selloff in AI and chip shares.
U.S. stocks closed sharply lower Friday, with the Nasdaq 100 falling 5.61% on the day and 10.43% for the week, its worst since March 2020. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28%, wiping out its gains for the year, while the S&P 500 dropped 3.70% for its seventh straight decline. The Dow lost 950 points. ft.com
Nvidia fell 14.01% to $125.53 after Reuters reported that the SEC was probing its accounting. The selling reached across the AI trade, from the companies designing chips to the ones supplying memory, optical gear and power. Treasuries caught a bid, with the 10-year yield down 12 basis points to 4.93%. Even with yields moving lower, tech shares remained under pressure.
U.S. closing levels
- Dow Industrial Average −950.10 points (−1.93%) to 48,151.82. Week −8.03%.
- S&P 500 −265.44 points (−3.70%) to 6,910.39. Week −8.61%.
- Nasdaq Composite −1,261.47 points (−5.28%) to 22,617.73. Week −10.02%.
- Russell 2000 −73.32 points (−2.76%) to 2,581.79. Week −7.48%.
- Nasdaq 100 −1,488.07 points (−5.61%) to 25,028.98. Week −10.43%.
The Dow had its worst week since March 2020. The Nasdaq Composite’s 10.02% loss was in line with its worst week in the spring 2025 selloff, while the S&P 500 had its worst week since that stretch. Friday’s breadth showed how far the selling spread. Nearly five Nasdaq stocks fell for every one that rose, and S&P 500 decliners outnumbered advancers 357 to 125.
The two Nasdaq levels to watch next week
The Nasdaq Composite closed at 22,617.73, just 99.82 points above its 100-week moving average at 22,517.91. The Nasdaq 100 finished at 25,028.98, just 111.63 points above its own 100-week moving average at 24,917.35. Both cushions are less than 0.5%.
Sellers have the short-term bias after a week like this. The two moving averages give buyers a place to lean against, but they need to hold those levels and put some distance between price and support. If both indices get below their averages and stay below, the bearish bias increases. On a rebound, I’d watch whether Nasdaq breadth improves alongside the indices.
Double-digit losses across the AI trade
Twenty-two names on the AI and chip watchlist fell more than 10% Friday, including the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, which dropped 10.60%. The losses reached across the AI buildout.
- AI cloud and infrastructure — Nebius −16.11%, CoreWeave −12.02%.
- Chip design and compute — Arm −14.09%, Nvidia −14.01%, AMD −13.25%, Broadcom −12.19%.
- Memory and storage — SanDisk −16.05%, Micron −13.89%, Western Digital −12.02%.
- Networking and optics — Credo −15.20%, Lumentum −13.94%, Coherent −12.90%, Arista Networks −11.57%.
- Power and chipmaking equipment — Bloom Energy −15.26%, Applied Materials −10.71%, KLA −10.33%, Lam Research −10.02%.
Trading education. Let support define your risk
If you’re leaning against a weekly moving average, decide what would invalidate the trade before you enter. A quick dip followed by a reclaim can tell you sellers had their shot and missed. A break followed by a failed rally back above the average tells you sellers are defending the level. The same moving average can help you define risk in either direction.

decisions.headline: European stocks end a bruising week. German DAX falls 7.29%.
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: News] European stocks end a bruising week. German DAX falls 7.29%.
The DAX posts its worst week since late March 2025. The major indices in France, the UK, Spain and Italy have their worst week since March 2026.
As London and European traders head home for the weekend, the major indices are closing sharply lower. The German DAX led the way down on Friday with a 2.60% decline, followed by Italy’s FTSE MIB at 2.48%. The UK’s FTSE 100 held up best on the day but still lost just over 1%.
Friday’s closing levels
- German DAX — 24,801.22, down 2.60%
- France’s CAC 40 — 7,927.75, down 1.89%
- UK FTSE 100 — 10,346.33, down 1.02%
- Spain’s IBEX 35 — 18,873.09, down 1.63%
- Italy’s FTSE MIB — 48,703.73, down 2.48%
For the trading week
- German DAX — down 7.29%, worst week since late March 2025
- Italy’s FTSE MIB — down 6.08%, worst week since March 2026
- Spain’s IBEX 35 — down 5.73%, worst week since March 2026
- France’s CAC 40 — down 5.27%, worst week since March 2026
- UK FTSE 100 — down 5.10%, worst week since March 2026
The DAX stands out. It lost more than a full percentage point more than Italy’s FTSE MIB on the week, and the decline was steep enough to exceed its March 2026 selloff. Even the FTSE 100, the best performer of the five, fell more than 5% for the week.
European 10-year yields fall across the board
The selloff in European equities came alongside a rally in government bonds. Benchmark 10-year yields fell in all five markets on Friday and finished lower for the week. UK yields led the weekly move, falling 9.5 basis points, followed by Germany at 8.8 basis points. Italy saw the smallest weekly decline at 2.1 basis points.
- Germany — 3.302% at the close, down 9.5 bps Friday and 8.8 bps for the week. The high for the week was at 3.421%. The low at 3.294%
- France — 4.872%, down 6.0 bps Friday and 5.7 bps for the week. The high for the week was at 4.972% which the low was at 4.835%
- UK — 5.243%, down 7.8 bps Friday and 9.5 bps for the week. The high was at 5.397%. The low at 5.227%
- Spain — 3.906%, down 8.6 bps Friday and 3.2 bps for the week. The high was at 4.009%. The low at 3.90%
- Italy — 4.408%, down 7.1 bps Friday and 2.1 bps for the week. The high was at 4.492%. The low at 4.400%.
With German yields falling more than their French yields the spread widened to 157 bps

[FULL UPDATED ARTICLE TEXT]
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] Fed’s Cook says monetary policy isn’t restrictive enough
Cook says the September rate hike fell short and warns that waiting raises the risk of inflation becoming embedded
The Fed’s Cook weighed in on inflation, the labor market and the need for tighter monetary policy in remarks that crossed the wires.
- Fed’s current monetary policy stance is not providing needed restraint.
- September’s interest rate hike was not enough to curtail high inflation.
- High inflation does not give U.S. central bank space to be patient.
- Holding off on rate hikes increases risk that inflation will embed in economy.
- Data since September points to need for tighter monetary policy.
- Current level of inflation is of “great concern.”
- U.S. economic growth is strong, labor market is healthy and stable.
- Embedded inflation will require more aggressive Fed response.
- Financial conditions are too accommodative right now.
- Tariff impact on inflation has faded.
- Little evidence AI is weighing on job market so far.
Analysis
These are hawkish comments from Cook. In her view, the September hike didn’t deliver enough restraint, and financial conditions are still too easy. With growth strong and the labor market holding up, she sees room for the Fed to tighten further. decisions.headline: Cook, The U.S. Economy in Global Context
decisions.raw_text:
[FED] [Categories: Speech] Cook, The U.S. Economy in Global Context
Speech At the XXIX Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile, Santiago, Chile
November 20, 2026
The U.S. Economy in Global Context
Governor Lisa D. Cook
At the XXIX Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile, Santiago, Chile
Share
Watch Live
Thank you, Governor Costa, for that kind introduction and for the invitation to deliver this keynote address and to participate in the 29th Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile today.1 It is a distinct privilege to be back in Santiago. I first came to Chile between my second and third years as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley after completing a summer as an intern at the World Bank. I was on a quest to determine whether economic growth in Latin America or in another region of the world would be the subject of my dissertation. It piqued my interest in inflation targeting, a sound fiscal framework, and now, of course, how to think about the economic forces reshaping the global economy. I am grateful for the chance to continue to learn from your experience and to share some of my own thinking.
I want to begin by acknowledging a fact that may seem obvious but is easy to overlook in the day-to-day work of setting monetary policy: The U.S. economy does not sit in isolation. As a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, my mandate is domestic—to promote maximum employment and price stability in the United States. But achieving that mandate requires that I pay careful attention to global developments, including economic and financial developments in Chile and across Latin America. The forces reconfiguring your economies are, in many cases, identical to the forces reconfiguring ours, even if they arrive on our respective shores somewhat differently.
Geopolitics and Trade
Let me start with geopolitical events. Over the past several years, the global economy has absorbed a remarkable sequence of shocks. Russia's war in Ukraine disrupted energy and commodity markets worldwide. The conflict in the Middle East pushed up energy prices again this year, and experts have warned that damaged infrastructure and depleted inventories could keep oil prices elevated for an extended period. These are not simply North American concerns. Oil is a globally traded commodity, and a conflict that drives up the price of oil in Houston drives it up in Santiago, as well. The precise transmission differs across countries, depending on whether they are net energy importers or exporters, but few economies have been insulated.
A related story applies to trade. Over the past two years, the U.S. has raised tariffs on a wide range of imports, and considerable uncertainty remains about where tariff levels will ultimately settle. In the U.S., the effects of tariffs on inflation appear to have moderated, even as uncertainty about future trade policy persists. China, too, has increased trade restrictions, limiting exports of critical minerals for which it supplies a large fraction of the world's production. These minerals are a crucial input, and uncertainty is rising around the world about access to them. I raise this not to make a judgment about trade policy—that is not my role—but because such shifts inevitably reverberate across the global economy. When trade relationships between major economies are altered, other countries must decide how to respond: whether to deepen commercial ties elsewhere, reconfigure supply chains, or wait for greater clarity before committing to new investment. These are decisions playing out in boardrooms and finance ministries around the world right now, including, I suspect, in some of the economies represented in this room.
The Global AI Buildout
The third global force I want to highlight—and the one I will spend the most time on—is the extraordinary buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure now underway around the world.

The University of Michigan’s monthly survey asks U.S. households about current economic conditions, the outlook and where they expect inflation to go. [FED] [Categories: Speech] Waller, Opening Remarks
Speech At the 2026 College Fed Challenge Finals, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Washington, D.C.
November 20, 2026
Opening Remarks
Governor Christopher J. Waller
At the 2026 College Fed Challenge Finals, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Washington, D.C.
Share
Thank you, Robin, and welcome, students and teachers, to the Federal Reserve Board.1
We are gathered for the finals of the annual College Fed Challenge, a tradition begun 23 years ago under Chairman Alan Greenspan. The challenge is to prepare and present a monetary policy recommendation that will best promote the Federal Reserve's dual mandate of stable prices and maximum sustainable employment. Students on the seven teams that will compete today represent the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Chicago; Cleveland State University; Harvard College; the University of Maryland, College Park; Pennsylvania State University; and St. Lawrence University.
Let me start by congratulating all of the students here today, and your faculty advisers, for advancing to the finals by winning preliminary rounds of the competition. A record 141 schools participated this year, from 34 states. It is incredibly gratifying to think of the number of young people motivated to learn about the Federal Reserve's role in promoting a healthy economy.
A few weeks from now, my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) and I will be sitting at this same table, facing the same challenge you face today. Like you, we will be examining publicly available data on economic and financial conditions and will apply our understanding of how monetary policy influences those conditions to render our best judgment of the policy stance that best furthers the Fed's goals.
Crucial to that decision will be clearly explaining the Committee's actions and intentions to the public—the same task that you will face later this morning, when you present your recommendations to our judges. As I hope you have learned, clear communication is essential because monetary policy works to a considerable extent by influencing the public's view of current and future economic and financial conditions.
Monetary policy has evolved since this competition began in 2003. At that time, the FOMC relied on a single tool to influence financial conditions and the broader economy—it set a target for the federal funds rate. In the years since, the Committee expanded its toolkit with unconventional policy tools.
In an important way, the competition you will engage in today is very much like what the FOMC does at its meetings. On December 8, my 18 FOMC colleagues and I will each present our view of the economic outlook, and on December 9, our view of the proper stance of monetary policy. Before we express those views to the public, we communicate with each other, presenting evidence, testing hypotheses, and making arguments that will ultimately help us arrive at a consensus that is summarized in our postmeeting statement. Every monetary policy speech I give has its origins in this room, in the argument I make here, and the extent to which that argument holds up to what I hear from my colleagues. When I engage in the essential task of explaining monetary policy to the public, I am really doing the same thing that I do here at FOMC meetings. And very much what you will do today. Present the evidence. Make an argument. Persuade.
I hope your preparations for this event have added to your understanding of the economy and the Federal Reserve's role and perhaps will even spur some of you to pursue further study of economics and finance. Among the talented individuals who are participating in today's challenge, I hope there are some who may one day contribute to our understanding of the economy and the work of the Fed. But I hope that all of you have benefited from this experience by adding to your knowledge a

decisions.headline: Gold's panic selling signals capitulation, but a catalyst is needed for a bottom
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Commodities] Gold's panic selling signals capitulation, but a catalyst is needed for a bottom
The latest gold's selloff might have been driven more by forced liquidations amid stock market losses than by deteriorating fundamentals, as the USD remained stable, real yields fell and rate hike expectations eased. The risk-reward for further downside is weakening, but a bullish catalyst is still missing. Monday's US Flash PMIs could provide one. Weaker data may trigger another dovish repricing further out the curve and support gold, while stronger figures could put some more downward pressure.
Gold extended the
selloff further despite no changes in the fundamentals. In fact, the US dollar
remained relatively flat, real yields fell a bit and rate hike expectations
actually eased following another rout in the stock market.
This mix would
generally support gold, but it looks like we got another liquidation caused by
stock market losses.
To understand the
mechanics, imagine that an investment fund holds stocks, gold and government
bonds. Some stocks suddenly crash, and the fund suffers losses on leveraged
positions. The fund may need to raise cash to meet margin calls, reduce
leverage or satisfy investor redemptions. Rather than selling only the assets
that caused the losses, it may sell whatever it can liquidate quickly. Gold is
particularly useful in this situation because it is highly liquid and can be
sold quickly.
The hawkish
repricing is now over, and we might even see a dovish repricing in the next
months if the equity losses extend further and economic data deteriorates. Therefore,
the risk-reward for more downside has weakened, although we haven’t got any
bullish catalyst yet to position for a reversal. Waiting for catalysts is always
better than trying to catch falling knives.
On Monday, we get
the Flash US PMIs. The data might provide the first bullish catalyst if it
surprises to the downside as growth concerns may increase further and rate hike
bets further down the curve should be unwound. A strong report, though, might
add some more downward pressure.
GOLD TECHNICAL
ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME
On the daily chart, we can
see that gold (CFD contract) extended the
losses even further and almost tested the 3,500 level. We can expect the buyers
to step in around the level, with a defined risk below it, to position for a
rally into the 4,700 level. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a
break to increase the bearish bets into the 3,100 level next.
GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4
HOUR TIMEFRAME
On the 4 hour chart, we
have a downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. If we get a pullback,
we can expect the sellers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above
it, to keep targeting new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see
the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the major downward
trendline around the 4,050 level next.
GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1
HOUR TIMEFRAME
On the 1 hour chart, we have
another minor trendline defining the bearish momentum on this timeframe. The sellers
will likely lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep
pushing into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break
higher to increase the bullish bets into the next trendline. The red lines
define the average daily range for today.
UPCOMING CATALYSTS
Today we have Trump speaking
at a press conference about his Asia trip, but he could certainly digress and
talk about Iran. On Monday, we get the US Flash PMIs. On Thursday, we get the latest
US Jobless Claims figures. The focus will remain on growth concerns, the Fed
and US-Iran developments.
Source URL: https://investinglive.com/commodities/gold-s-panic-selling-signals-capitulation-but-a-catalyst-is-needed-for-a-bottom/

decisions.headline: Christine Lagarde: Acting in time — - SPEECH

[ECB] Christine Lagarde: Acting in time
- SPEECH
Acting in time
Keynote speech by Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, at the 36th Frankfurt European Banking Congress
Frankfurt am Main, 20 November 2026
It is a pleasure to be back at this congress. This is the eighth time I have spoken here as President of the ECB, and it will sadly be the last.
In preparing for today, I reread those speeches. The topics have varied, from growth and inflation to capital markets and the Single Market.
But one concern runs through all of them: how to make Europe stronger, so that its prosperity is driven by its own strengths and less exposed to decisions taken elsewhere.
For many years, the challenges we discussed here were old ones. We had fallen short of our ambitions for the Single Market. Our growth relied too heavily on external demand for an economy of our size, and our competitiveness was slowly eroding.
Those challenges have not gone away. But in recent years, new ones have been layered on top. Dependencies that we once saw as a normal part of an open economy, from critical raw materials to technology, can now be used against us. That has made economic sovereignty a challenge in its own right.
The old challenges and the new ones have something in common.
Five centuries ago, Machiavelli compared the problems of states to a fever that, at the start, is “easy to cure but difficult to detect” and, in time, becomes “easy to detect but difficult to cure”.
Both kinds of challenge are of this sort. By the time everyone can see the need to act, the best time to act has usually passed.
Acting early, before the case is obvious, is one of the hardest things a policymaker has to do. It means paying a price up front for a distant pay-off. And if nothing goes wrong, those who acted can easily appear to have paid that price for nothing.
Today I would like to reflect on how Europe can still act early, drawing on how we have approached this at the ECB and on what I have learned along the way.
Why Europe acts in some crises but not others
It is often said that Europe only moves in a crisis. Jean Monnet wrote that Europe would be forged in crises, and would be the sum of the solutions adopted for them. The idea was that Europe has a kind of in-built inertia that only a crisis can overcome.
My experience of the past seven years is that this is only partly true. Europe responds decisively to some crises and hesitantly to others.
When events convince us that the world has changed, we act. During my term, I have watched Europe break one taboo after another.
Before the pandemic, few believed that the EU would ever borrow on a large scale in its own name. But once we accepted that no country could recover on its own, we created a recovery fund financed by common debt to the tune of €800 billion.
Europe was also said to be unable to take its own security seriously. Yet when Germany concluded that it would have to take on more of its own defence, it made the biggest change to its defence spending in generations. At the European level, we also agreed on Security Action for Europe (SAFE), which offers up to €150 billion in loans for joint defence procurement. And after decades of neutrality, Finland and Sweden joined NATO.
Nor did many expect Europe to act as a geopolitical power. Yet it is now Ukraine’s largest supporter. And when it became clear that Europe would have to bear more of the cost, the countries ready to act found a new way to borrow together on Ukraine’s behalf, even though not every country was ready to take part. Hence the coalition of the willing.
What made these steps possible? In each case, the cost of inaction was there for all to see, and it was plainly greater than the cost of acting. Once we were convinced of that, our institutions did not hold us back.

decisions.headline: Paulson tells Q&A the Fed has more tightening to do, after a speech with no rate steer
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] Paulson tells Q&A the Fed has more tightening to do, after a speech with no rate steer
After a guidance-free speech, Fed’s Paulson told a Q&A the Fed has more tightening to do, at a deliberate pace that lets the economy adjust. She said inflation is too high, the job market is at full employment and lowering inflation is the priority.
The key idea
- The Federal Reserve is signaling that interest rates will continue to rise to combat high inflation.
- This policy of "tightening" means making money more expensive to borrow, which slows down economic activity and ideally brings down prices.
- A "hawkish lean" indicates that policymakers are more concerned about inflation and are inclined to favor higher interest rates.
Reader questions
- What does "quarter-point December pricing" mean for investors? It means that financial markets are expecting the Fed to raise its benchmark interest rate by 0.25% at its December meeting.
- Why would continued rate hikes be a "headwind for gold"? When interest rates rise, assets like bonds become more attractive because they offer better returns, making non-yielding assets like gold less appealing to investors.
- What is the significance of the Fed moving at a "deliberate pace"? A deliberate pace suggests the Fed prefers smaller, more frequent rate increases, allowing the economy time to adjust and avoiding sudden shocks.
Paulson’s comments confirm the hawkish lean that her prepared remarks left unsaid, which supports quarter-point December pricing and the view that hikes continue into 2027. Her emphasis on a deliberate pace argues against Waller’s 50 basis point idea, so the comments are more likely to firm up 2027 pricing than lift odds of a jumbo move. That combination supports front-end Treasury yields and the dollar. It’s another headwind for gold, which is already being sold toward $3,600.

[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Stock market update] UBS cuts global stocks to Neutral, days after Morgan Stanley went maximum overweight
UBS cut global equities to Neutral in its 2027 outlook, citing high expectations, AI uncertainty and a top 10 making up 39% of the S&P 500. It prefers bonds and commodities, likes Eurozone stocks and urges investors to refocus rather than retreat.
The key idea
- Major investment banks can have very different views on the future direction of the stock market, even when looking at the same economic information.
- This article highlights a disagreement between UBS and Morgan Stanley on how much risk investors should take in global stocks for 2027.
- A "Neutral" rating, as given by UBS, suggests that the potential rewards from an investment are balanced by its risks, meaning it is not strongly recommended to buy or sell.
Reader questions
- Why do these differing opinions from big banks matter to investors?
The opinions of large investment banks can influence market sentiment and investor decisions, as many investors look to these institutions for guidance. Their differing views show that even experts can disagree on market outlooks, emphasizing the importance of individual research.
- What does "concentration in AI-linked megacaps" mean and why is it a concern?
This refers to a large portion of the stock market's value being held by a few very big companies, especially those involved in Artificial Intelligence. It is a concern because if these few large companies face problems, it can have a disproportionately large negative impact on the overall market.
- What is an "equal-weight US strategy" and why would UBS recommend it?
An equal-weight strategy means investing the same amount of money in each stock within an index, rather than weighting them by their market size. UBS recommends this to reduce reliance on the largest technology stocks and diversify investments more broadly across the market.
The split between two tier-one houses underlines how finely balanced the 2027 equity case is. Concentration in AI-linked megacaps is the fault line. UBS’s preference for the Eurozone, equal-weight US strategies, industrials and health care points to rotation rather than outright selling, which could cushion broader indices even if tech leaders struggle. Higher-for-longer Fed rates and yields above 5% remain the key risk to valuations, so the December 9 Fed decision and the rate path into 2027 matter for both views. For Asia, where AI and chip stocks dominate several indices, UBS’s concentration warning is particularly relevant after Thursday's, now Friday’s, selloff.

decisions.headline: No, the Fed isn’t pumping $1.756 billion into markets on Friday morning: what that viral post gets wrong
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Stocks] No, the Fed isn’t pumping $1.756 billion into markets on Friday morning: what that viral post gets wrong
Posts doing the rounds claiming the Fed will inject $1.756bn of liquidity are misleading.
There was an operation, on Wednesday! It was a routine, pre-scheduled NY Fed T-bill purchase that reinvests maturing holdings, adding no net liquidity. In all, about $14bn is scheduled to December 11.
The key idea
- The article clarifies that a reported "liquidity injection" by the Federal Reserve was a routine, pre-scheduled Treasury bill purchase.
- This type of operation, called a reinvestment purchase, replaces maturing securities in the Fed's portfolio.
- Reinvestment purchases do not expand the Fed's balance sheet or add new money to the financial system.
Reader questions
- What is the difference between reinvestment purchases and reserve management purchases? Reinvestment purchases simply swap one asset for another, keeping the Fed's balance sheet size the same. Reserve management purchases, however, do expand the balance sheet and add net new reserves to the system.
- Why does the timing of these operations matter? These operations are routine and pre-scheduled, meaning they are not a response to current market volatility or a signal of new policy. This helps avoid misinterpretations by the market.
- How can I verify information about the Fed's operations? You can check the New York Fed's published schedule and results pages, which show the planned and actual sizes of all their operations.
These operations are pre-announced, small relative to the Treasury market and reserve-neutral, so they carry no policy signal. The real liquidity story is the Fed’s hiking path (eg. J.P. Morgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call ) and year-end funding conditions, where rising net bill supply, not these purchases, is the main influence on reserves. Traders watching for genuine balance sheet signals should focus on any change in the Desk’s language about reserve conditions, or a return of reserve management purchases.
---

- A significant drop in US technology stocks, especially those related to Artificial Intelligence, can trigger similar declines in Asian markets heavily invested in the same sector.

- Why would a long weekend in Japan add to selling pressure? A long weekend means markets are closed for an extended period, and investors might sell their holdings beforehand to avoid being exposed to potential negative news or market movements while they cannot trade.
The selloff is concentrated in the AI supply chain, so chip-heavy indices like the Nikkei, the KOSPI and Taiwan’s market are the most exposed if US tech fails to steady. With Tokyo shut until Tuesday, Japanese exposure is likely to be hedged through Nikkei futures trading offshore, which could amplify moves. [INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Commodities] Gold slides toward $3,600 as sellers press on, but UBS upgrades it and still sees $5,000
Gold is being sold heavily again, slipping to around $3,606 as Fed hike bets build. UBS has upgraded it to Attractive in its 2027 outlook, seeing $5,000 by December 2027 as real yields ease, though it has pushed that target back from mid-2027.
The key idea
- Gold prices are currently falling due to expectations of continued interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, which makes holding gold less attractive.
- Real yields are a key concept here; they represent the return an investor gets on a bond after accounting for inflation. When real yields rise, non-interest bearing assets like gold become less appealing.

- Why is the $3,600 level important for gold? This level is being tested as a potential support point; if gold falls below it, there might be little to stop further declines until the next support level around $3,500.
UBS’s upgrade gives longer-term buyers a reason to look at gold at these levels. But the near-term flow still belongs to rates, and nothing in the call changes the picture before the December 9 Fed decision. The low $3,600s are now being tested, and a clean break would leave the market with little obvious support until the high $3,500s. A short-covering bounce is possible if US data soften or the dollar pauses, but rallies are likely to meet selling while three-hike forecasts keep spreading.

[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] Fed's Paulson keeps quiet on December, says October’s pause was never meant as a stop
Fed’s Paulson gave no near-term rate steer in New York, arguing understanding beats guidance and that October’s pause was never a stop. Last week she backed further gradual hikes and named three triggers that would make her favour moving faster.
The key idea
- The Federal Reserve aims for clear communication so markets understand its intentions, even without explicit future guidance.
- This approach, called "reaction function" communication, means the Fed expects markets to predict its actions based on economic data.
- A "pause" in rate hikes does not necessarily mean the Fed has stopped raising rates; it can be a temporary hold before further increases.
Reader questions
- Why does the Fed prefer markets to understand its "reaction function" instead of giving direct guidance? The Fed believes that if markets understand its decision making process, policy can be more predictable and effective, requiring less direct communication.
- What are the "three triggers" Paulson mentioned for faster rate hikes? Paulson identified rising inflation expectations, increasing wage growth, and higher underlying inflation as signals that would make her favor quicker interest rate increases.
- Why is the December payrolls report important in this context? The December payrolls report will provide data on wage growth, one of the key triggers Paulson mentioned, which traders will watch for clues about the Fed's next move.
With no fresh policy signal, the speech is unlikely to move rate pricing, and a quarter-point December hike remains the strong favourite. Her “pause was not a stop” framing supports the view that the hiking cycle runs into 2027, which keeps front-end Treasury yields and the dollar supported. Her three triggers for faster hikes give traders a checklist for the 4 December payrolls report and other data before the meeting: inflation expectations, wage growth and underlying inflation. An upside surprise on wages or expectations would strengthen the case for the larger move that Waller has floated.

The euro has fallen below $1.10 to an 18-month low, down about 6% since late August, with bearish bets the heaviest in over six years. Morgan Stanley and Deutsche Bank see $1.08 next year as French election risk and Fed hikes favour the dollar.
The key idea
- The euro is weakening against the dollar due to political uncertainty in France and the expectation of continued interest rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve.
- "Short positioning" means investors are betting a currency or asset will fall in value; when many investors do this, the market is said to be "stretched" or "crowded."

- What is the "intervention zone near 160" for USD/JPY? This refers to a level where the Japanese government or central bank might step in to buy yen and sell dollars to prevent their currency from weakening too much.
With short positioning this stretched, the euro is vulnerable to sharp short-covering rallies even if the trend stays lower. A credible French budget or a soft US inflation reading would be the likeliest triggers. On the downside, the $1.08 to $1.09 area is the next focus, where the bank forecasts and options-market risk sit. - The article suggests that the Federal Reserve's strategy of smaller, more frequent interest rate hikes could support the dollar more effectively than one large, immediate hike.

[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Commodities] Gold at $3,625: five forces behind the sell-off, and four reasons buyers haven’t quit
Gold slumps to around $3,625, 35% below January’s record, as a hiking Fed, 5% yields and a firm dollar keep sellers in charge. Central bank buying, record global ETF holdings and China’s retail demand keep the longer-term bull case alive for now.
The key idea
- The price of gold is currently caught in a tug of war between strong selling pressures and persistent buying interest.
- Selling pressures are mainly driven by rising interest rates and a strong US dollar, which make gold less attractive compared to other investments.
- Gold pays no interest, so when interest rates rise elsewhere, holding gold becomes more costly relative to other assets that do offer a return.
Reader questions
- Why do rising interest rates hurt gold prices? When interest rates go up, investments like bonds offer higher returns, making them more appealing than gold, which does not pay any interest or dividends. This reduces demand for gold, pushing its price down.
- How does a strong US dollar affect gold? Gold is typically priced in US dollars, so when the dollar strengthens, it makes gold more expensive for buyers using other currencies. This can reduce demand from international buyers, contributing to lower gold prices.
- Why are central banks buying gold if prices are falling? Central banks often buy gold as a long term store of value and to diversify their reserves, rather than for short term trading gains. Their purchases reflect a strategic view of gold's role in a national portfolio, not a reaction to daily price movements.
Gold now trades below most major bank year-end targets, leaving it oversold on fundamentals but without a catalyst to turn it. With the $3,700 handle gone, traders are looking for support in the low $3,600s and high $3,500s, and a clean break would invite more momentum selling. The December 9 Fed decision is the main event risk: a 50 basis point hike or a higher dot plot would extend losses, while any hint the cycle is near its end could spark a sharp short-covering bounce. Miners are still far above record production costs, so margins can absorb further weakness, and supply is unlikely to tighten from producers cutting output.

[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] J.P. Morgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call
J.P. Morgan now sees 25bp Fed hikes in January and March on top of December, taking rates to 4.50%-4.75%. It says sticky inflation, not jobs, is the driver, and that hikes protect credibility as the Fed lacks a convincing case to pause next year.
The key idea
- Major financial institutions like J.P. Morgan regularly update their economic forecasts, and these changes can signal shifts in market expectations.
- The "federal funds rate" is the target interest rate set by the U.S. central bank, the Federal Reserve; changes to this rate influence borrowing costs across the economy.
- "Tightening" refers to the Fed's policy of raising interest rates to slow down economic growth and combat inflation.
Reader questions
- What does "sticky inflation" mean, and why is it important here? Sticky inflation refers to prices that are slow to adjust downwards, even when economic conditions change; it suggests that inflation might be more persistent than previously thought, leading the Fed to continue raising rates.
- Why does the Fed's "credibility" matter for these rate hikes? The Fed's credibility is its ability to effectively manage the economy and achieve its goals, like stable prices; if the market doubts the Fed's commitment to fighting inflation, it could lead to higher inflation expectations and make the Fed's job harder.
- How do these predicted rate hikes affect Treasury yields and the dollar? Higher expected interest rates generally make U.S. Treasury bonds more attractive to investors, pushing up their yields; a stronger dollar often follows, as higher rates can draw foreign capital seeking better returns.
A tier-one house moving from one more hike to three adds weight to the view that tightening doesn’t end in December, which supports two-year Treasury yields and the dollar. Pricing for 2027 is now where the action is, so January and March contracts are likely to firm. Strength against the yen is limited by a likely BoJ hike and intervention risk near 160. - Magnificent Seven — Amazon −3.87%, Alphabet −3.46%, Nvidia −3.30%, Meta −3.27%, Tesla −2.43%, Microsoft −1.97% and Apple −0.92%.
- AI and chip stocks — Nebius Group −9.39%, AMD −7.72% and CoreWeave −6.11%. Intel bucked the selling, gaining 1.92%.
- Other standouts — Ambarella +7.85%, Palo Alto Networks +6.42%, Western Digital +2.98% and CrowdStrike +2.71%.
- Other laggards — Zoom Communications −9.56%, Celsius −6.20%, Block −6.02%, DoorDash −5.80%, SharkNinja −5.75%, Nike −5.43% and Shopify −5.34%.
Other winners...Anthropic Employees
Anthropic’s IPO added roughly $7.7 million per employee in paper gains from the $83 offering price to the $97.17 first-day close. That lifted the estimated average value of employee equity awards from about $44 million to $52 million, before taxes. The estimate uses The Wall Street Journal’s tally of stock options and restricted stock across roughly 5,300 employees. wsj.com
The $52 million is an average equity value. Actual cash proceeds are unknown, and the filing doesn’t disclose the median employee’s holdings. Awards vary widely, and vesting and lockups limit when employees can sell.
Trading lesson. Use breadth to check the bounce.
If the S&P or Nasdaq bounces next session, watch whether more stocks start participating and whether that improvement holds. A handful of large stocks can lift an index while most names are still under pressure. After a day when S&P 500 decliners outnumbered advancers by roughly 12 to 1, a sustained improvement in breadth would give buyers more evidence that they’re taking back some control.

decisions.headline: More from Fed’s Goolsbee: AI boom a ‘pig through the python’ that risks overheating US economy
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] More from Fed’s Goolsbee: AI boom a ‘pig through the python’ that risks overheating US economy
Chicago Fed’s Goolsbee says AI-driven investment and wealth gains risk overheating the US economy and adding to inflation he calls borderline disturbingly high, with demand, not just oil and tariffs, driving it. He sees no clear path back to 2% yet.
The key idea
- The main idea is that the rapid growth in artificial intelligence (AI) investment and related stock market gains could lead to the US economy growing too quickly. This rapid growth might then cause inflation to remain high, making it harder for the Federal Reserve to reach its 2% target.
- "Overheating" an economy means that demand for goods and services is growing faster than the economy's ability to produce them. This imbalance typically leads to rising prices, or inflation.
Reader questions
- What does "demand side argument" mean for the Fed? A demand side argument suggests that inflation is being driven by strong consumer and business spending, rather than just problems with supply. This often signals to the Fed that they may need to raise interest rates to cool down the economy.
- Why is services inflation important here? Services inflation is closely watched because it tends to reflect underlying demand in the economy more directly than goods prices, which can be heavily influenced by global supply chains or commodity costs like oil. If services inflation is high, it suggests strong domestic demand.
- What is a "tail risk for stocks"? A tail risk is a low probability event that, if it occurs, could have a very significant negative impact. In this context, a major correction in AI related stocks is a tail risk because it could unexpectedly and severely affect the broader stock market and financial stability.
Goolsbee’s remarks add a demand-side argument to a Fed debate already leaning toward hikes. Markets heavily favour a quarter-point move on December 9, and a voice outside the usual hawks warning of overheating supports front-end yields and the dollar. He says inflation is not just an oil and tariff story, so a pullback in crude would ease less of the pressure than traders might hope. His uncertainty about how banks would cope with an AI-led equity correction marks a tail risk for stocks that could quickly reverse the tightening narrative.

decisions.headline: Fed’s Goolsbee says he sees no clear path back to 2% inflation
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] Fed’s Goolsbee says he sees no clear path back to 2% inflation
He says the path for interest rates depends on whether inflation moves back toward target and points to data center demand and AI-related wealth as sources of price pressure.
Goolsbee’s comments on inflation, interest rates and AI investment crossed the wires.
- What is happening with services inflation is important in understanding whether price pressures stem from demand or things like energy costs.
- Inflation has proven to be far more persistent than was thought in 2025, and data center demand and AI-related wealth impact is adding to it.
- The steepness of the interest-rate path will be rooted in whether “borderline disturbingly high” inflation is seen returning to Fed’s 2% target.
- Does not see at this point that inflation is on the path back to 2%. It is not just coming from oil and tariff shocks, but a sizable demand component.
- Is not concerned about wages pressuring inflation at this point.
- It has not been good news on inflation for the past few months.
- Anthropic’s IPO raises the question of how stockholders will use that wealth. It could have a macroeconomic impact.
- Artificial intelligence is influencing today’s economy through wealth impacts and investment.
- There is widespread acknowledgment among businesses that costs are up, particularly among firms in construction or competing with data centers for components.
- Is not sure if fallout from US midterm elections will include a slowdown in data-center buildout or have a lasting impact on equity prices.
- More openness about monetary policy has been productive for the Fed and the world.
- Consumer spending has been pretty broad-based, financed mostly out of income growth.
- There is a high risk that economy’s capacity cannot handle the current “pig-through-the-python” level of business investment without overheating.
- Not clear how financial sector would be impacted if there is a major correction in equities related to AI.
Analysis
The takeaway is hawkish. Goolsbee sees a sizable demand component to inflation, which makes it harder for the Fed to look through the recent price pressure. Businesses are already reporting higher costs where they compete with data centers for components, and he sees a risk that the economy has trouble absorbing the current pace of investment without overheating.
Services inflation is the barometer to watch. If it stays sticky even as energy pressures ease, that would strengthen the case that demand is keeping inflation elevated and give the Fed more reason to tighten. If services inflation cools, the case for a steeper rate path weakens.
Source URL: https://investinglive.com/central-banks/fed-s-goolsbee-says-he-sees-no-clear-path-back-to-2-inflation/

[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] Fed's Goolsbee: Job market is stable, but inflation is "way higher" than Fed's 2% target
Inflation from the war. Inflation from the tariffs. If you have both, you will have inflation.
Comments from Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, a 2027 FOMC voter, crossed the wires on inflation, jobs and consumer demand.
- The impact of tariffs has been more persistent than expected.
- The job market is stable, but inflation is “way higher” than the Fed’s 2% target. Consumer demand has been very strong and solid.
- AI seems promising as a boost to productivity but the day job of the Fed is to determine if the economy is overheating now
- The job market is stable.
- The Fed failure has been on inflation.
- Changes in immigration policy means the Fed should put less weight on monthly job numbers as a signal about the business cycle.
- Fed is still looking for evidence AI driven productivity is starting to move beyond the tech sector.
- Unless AI shows a can increase productivity outside the tech sector, it could prove a flash in the pan.
Analysis
The tone is hawkish. If tariffs are still feeding through to prices, one source of inflation may take longer to fade. At the same time, solid consumer demand gives businesses room to pass along higher costs, and a stable job market gives the Fed room to keep its focus on inflation. For traders, the question heading into December is whether the inflation data make the case for a faster pace of tightening.
Remember the Fed did nothing at the end of October meeting most likely due to the elections in early November. The minutes of the meeting were more hawkish yesterday.
In the absence of the election, would the Fed have tightened? My guess is yes. So 50 bps in December would get the Fed to what would be the normal progression given the inflation threat. If the Fed is failing on inflation, do something about it.
The market is still only implying a small 5.6% chance for a 50 bp hike in December (it has been up at about 10% recently).
What other Fed officials said this week
- Christopher Waller, Nov. 18 — Inflation is spreading across more categories, with roughly 70% of core services items running above 3%. He warned that businesses could start treating 3% as normal and made the case for a 50-basis-point hike in December or a clear signal that rates would rise faster in the months ahead.
- Mary Daly, Nov. 18 — Inflation has been too high for too long, and its path remains uncertain. She described the labor market as stable and said spending was holding up even among lower-income households. images.investinglive.com
- Alberto Musalem, Nov. 17 — The risks tilt toward inflation staying above 2%. He said several rate increases would likely be needed before spring 2027 and argued that moving sooner could help bring inflation down while expectations are still anchored.
- Beth Hammack, Nov. 16 — Inflation pressures are worsening, but she still favors slow, steady rate hikes and sees little reason to accelerate the pace at this point.

[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Stocks] European stocks close lower. Anthropic opens 34% above its IPO price.
Spain’s IBEX 35 leads the declines in Europe, French yields jump 7.5 basis points, and the Nasdaq holds its gains as the Dow falls more than 400 points.
European stocks finish lower across the board
As London and European traders head for the exits, the major indices are all lower. Spain’s IBEX 35 led the declines, while the UK’s FTSE 100 and Germany’s DAX each fell a little over 0.9%. Italy’s FTSE MIB held up the best of the group, but still lost 0.46%.
- German DAX −0.92% to 25,498.90
- France’s CAC 40 −0.81% to 8,080.74
- UK FTSE 100 −0.93% to 10,452.68
- Spain’s IBEX 35 −0.97% to 19,186.20
- Italy’s FTSE MIB −0.46% to 49,941.24
French yields lead the move higher
European 10-year yields rose across the board, with France leading the way. The French 10-year rose 7.5 basis points to 4.942% (the high for the cycle reached in October extended to 5.142%), while Germany’s rose 4.0 basis points to 3.412% (recent high at 3.653%). That widened the French-German spread by 3.5 basis points to 153 basis points (high at 176 bps).
Elsewhere, Spain’s 10-year rose 5.1 basis points to 3.999%, Italy’s rose 3.1 basis points to 4.489%, and the UK’s rose 2.6 basis points to 5.329%.
Anthropic opens at $111.50. The Dow falls more than 400 points.
Anthropic’s first trade on the Nasdaq came in at $111.50, up $28.50, or 34.3%, from its $83 IPO price. That was also above the earlier $104 indication. The shares traded as high as $115.10 and as low as $109.99, and were at $111.64 as European traders wrapped up their day.
The Nasdaq Composite was up 0.47% and the Nasdaq 100 was up 0.50% at the European close. The gains didn’t carry across the broader market. The Dow was down 442 points, or 0.88%, the Russell 2000 was down 0.59%, and the S&P 500 was just below unchanged, down 0.07%.
U.S. continuing claims jump as Philly Fed new orders slip below zero
Initial jobless claims rose by just 1K to 203K from a revised 202K, above the 197K estimate. The bigger move was in continuing claims, which jumped 70K to 1.763 million from 1.693 million, well above the 1.710 million estimate. The insured unemployment rate held at 1.1%. investinglive.com
The November Philly Fed manufacturing index fell to 6.3 from 20.9, well below the 20.0 estimate and the lowest reading since May. The headline stayed in expansion territory, but new orders fell to −0.4 from 4.3. Shipments and employment improved, while the prices-paid index jumped to 58.2 from 43.2 and prices received rose to 47.0. For the Fed, that’s a familiar mix of softer demand and persistent price pressure.
The Conference Board’s Leading Economic Index fell 0.3% in October after holding steady in September. Fewer building permits drove most of the decline, while the coincident index, which tracks current activity, was unchanged.
U.S. yields climb, led by the short end
Despite the softer data, Treasury yields were higher at the European close, with the bigger moves at the short end. The 2-year rose 3.4 basis points to 4.834%, the 5-year rose 2.7 basis points to 4.911%, and the 10-year rose 1.9 basis points to 5.085%. The 30-year was up 1.4 basis points at 5.426%.
USDJPY presses toward 160. Oil moves higher.
The dollar was mixed. USDJPY rose 0.35% to 159.89 after reaching 159.96, just shy of the 160.00 level. GBPUSD fell 0.25% to 1.3114, and AUDUSD was down 0.49% at 0.6684. EURUSD was little changed at 1.0981 after trading above 1.1000 earlier, while NZDUSD rose 0.31% to 0.5508 and USDCAD slipped 0.16% to 1.4303.
In commodities, WTI crude gained $1.44, or 1.73%, to $84.70, while Brent rose $1.02, or 1.11%, to $92.97.

decisions.headline: Jefferson, Monetary Policy amid Frequent and Complex Shocks
decisions.raw_text:
[FED] [Categories: Speech] Jefferson, Monetary Policy amid Frequent and Complex Shocks
Speech At the International Monetary Fund and Central Bank of Brazil Conference “A Quarter Century of Inflation Targeting in Latin America: Progress, Challenges, and the Road Ahead,” Brasília, Brazil
November 19, 2026
Monetary Policy amid Frequent and Complex Shocks
Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson
At the International Monetary Fund and Central Bank of Brazil Conference “A Quarter Century of Inflation Targeting in Latin America: Progress, Challenges, and the Road Ahead,” Brasília, Brazil
Share
Watch Live
Thank you, Nigel, for that kind introduction, and thank you to the Central Bank of Brazil and International Monetary Fund for hosting this important conference.1 It is an honor to be here with my fellow panelists. Today, I will briefly discuss issues that are critical for central bankers around the world—that is, how to assess and confront economic shocks. I discussed these issues in more depth in a speech earlier this year at Stanford University.2
Shocks, by their nature, are difficult to predict and vary in length, but we are nonetheless very familiar with them. Just in the past few years, we have experienced a pandemic, a rapid rise in energy prices associated with geopolitical tensions, changes to trade policy, and a technological breakthrough. One way to classify shocks is to determine whether their initial effect is on the demand side or the supply side of the economy. Demand shocks affect spending by households, businesses, or the government without changing productive capacity. Supply shocks change productive capacity—what economists call "potential output"—by affecting the available supply of labor and capital or the productivity of those inputs. The nature and duration of these shocks influence the approach to monetary policymaking.
As a monetary policymaker in the United States, I must consider whether and how shocks impact both sides of our dual mandate—maximum employment and stable prices. When a shock moves the output gap and inflation in the same direction, our objectives are aligned, and policy actions taken to address one also support the other.3 When a shock pushes them in opposite directions, there is a tradeoff. The recent rise in oil prices tied to the conflict in the Middle East is an example of the latter. An energy price shock can push up inflation while weighing on real incomes and demand. The appropriate response depends on the relative costs of missing each objective and the balance of risks. When the recent energy price shock occurred, inflation in the U.S. was already above our 2 percent target. If inflation expectations risk becoming unanchored, a stronger reaction to inflation is warranted. If price pressures are contained, it may be prudent to prioritize downside risks to employment.
Shocks that affect both aggregate supply and aggregated demand but with differential timing are especially challenging for monetary policymakers. The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) represents such a shock. Business adoption of AI has risen considerably over the past two years.4 On the demand side, optimism about the technology has been boosting business investment in data centers, advanced computing equipment, and related products. On the supply side, AI is likely to automate some tasks and augment others, which could raise productivity and, in turn, the growth rate of potential output. Currently, the AI buildout is exerting upward pressure on demand and inflation. In the future, advancements in productivity could exert downward pressure on inflation while continuing to support growth. Labor market effects are relevant as well. AI could cause some job displacement, a meaningful challenge for affected households. Like many technological breakthroughs of the past, however, AI could lead to the creation of new jobs and new firms that we have not yet imagined.
Shocks do not arrive in a vacuum. Energy, trade, and AI shock

[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: News] US initial jobless claims 203K vs 197K estimate
The weekly initial and continuing claims data.

US initial jobless claims rose by just 1,000 in the week ending November 14, but the result was 5,000 above expectations after the prior week was revised higher. The US Department of Labor released the figures at 8:30 a.m. ET on November 19. dol.gov
The bigger move was in continuing claims, which rose 70,000 in the week ending November 7. That could signal that people already receiving benefits are taking longer to find work. The four-week average also moved higher, while the insured unemployment rate held at 1.1%. Looking at the chart below, the spike higher sticks out but it is off low levels.
Quick analysis
The report leans softer, with continuing claims carrying more weight than the small rise in new filings. That would normally put some downward pressure on short-term Treasury yields and the US dollar. For the Fed, the question is whether continuing claims keep rising over the next few weeks. Initial claims still averaged fewer than 200,000 over the past four weeks, suggesting layoffs remain relatively limited. dol.gov
What this report measures
Initial claims count new applications for unemployment insurance and offer a timely gauge of layoffs. Continuing claims track ongoing benefit filings and are reported with an extra week’s lag. Traders watch the seasonally adjusted four-week averages to smooth out weekly swings and spot changes in the labor market that could influence Fed policy.

The Philadelphia Fed’s Manufacturing Business Outlook Survey is the oldest of the regional Fed factory surveys, dating to 1968, and one of the most closely watched. It’s released at 8:30 am ET on the third Thursday of the month and covers manufacturers in the Third Federal Reserve District: eastern Pennsylvania, southern New Jersey and Delaware.
The headline is the current general business activity index, which comes from a single question asking firms whether overall activity at their plant increased, decreased or held steady from the previous month. Unlike the Richmond survey, it isn’t a composite of other components. Like the other regional surveys, it’s a diffusion index, calculated as the percentage reporting an increase minus the percentage reporting a decrease, so zero marks the line between expansion and contraction.
The survey also tracks new orders, shipments, unfilled orders, delivery times, inventories, employment, the average workweek, prices paid and prices received. Each comes with a future index for expectations six months ahead. The prices paid index is watched as an early signal of input cost pressures, and the new orders index is a guide to where activity is headed. Most months include special questions on topics such as capital spending plans, wage growth, price expectations or the impact of tariffs.
The sample is relatively small, which makes the headline volatile and prone to large swings that don’t always reflect a change in trend. Even so, the Philly Fed survey tends to move markets more than other regional reports because of its long history and its track record alongside the national ISM manufacturing index.
It’s the second regional survey each month, after the Empire State report. The Philly Fed also publishes a nonmanufacturing survey later in the month.

The recent selloff in crude oil looks increasingly driven by demand concerns rather than improving supply expectations, as Middle East tensions remain elevated. Further downside will likely require additional pressure from weaker economic data, a more hawkish Fed or a broader stock market selloff.
Crude oil extended the
losses yesterday, with growth concerns looking increasingly as the likely culprit
given no change on the US-Iran front.
In fact, the Middle East
tensions remain elevated, with the risk of further escalation increasing. Trump
is reportedly weighing new strikes on Iran while insisting that the US does not
need outside help and that the blockade remains its most effective tool. US
officials also warned that Iran is prepared for further escalation and Israel
is pushing for action.
Meanwhile, the conflict
between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis continues, with both sides exchanging
attacks yesterday. Moreover, Saudi Arabia said that it expected the war against
the Houthis to last well into 2027.

whatsoever on the supply side expectations, so the demand side has to be
responsible for the recent selloff. There is certainly a scenario where oil

decisions.headline: FX option expiries for 19 November 10am New York cut
decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Forex Orders] FX option expiries for 19 November 10am New York cut
- A look at what is on the board for today
Q&A
- What exactly is an FX option expiry?
An FX option gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to exchange one currency for another at a predetermined exchange rate — known as the strike price — before or at a specified expiry.
- Why can a large expiry influence the spot market?
The key reason is hedging activity. Banks and option dealers that have sold options often hedge their exposure by buying or selling the underlying currency pair. As spot moves closer to the strike, those hedges may need to be adjusted. That can create additional buying or selling flows in the spot market.
- Does a large expiry automatically mean price will move towards the strike?
No. This is one of the most important points for traders. An option expiry is context, not a trading signal. Example: If EUR/USD is trading at 1.1600 and there is a large expiry at 1.1800, that expiry is unlikely to matter much on its own. But if EUR/USD is trading at 1.1790 with only a few hours remaining before expiry, the strike becomes considerably more relevant.
- What factors are important in viewing an FX option expiry?
The potential influence generally depends on several factors: Size of the expiry, distance between spot and the strike, time remaining until expiry, current market liquidity, and whether there are stronger macro or headline-driven forces at work.
- Can option expiries act as support or resistance?
Sometimes. A large strike can temporarily behave like support, resistance or a magnet because of hedging flows. But this should not be confused with traditional technical support or resistance. Once the option expires, the effect may disappear entirely.
- What is the main takeaway?
FX option expiries do not tell traders where the market must go. Instead, they can help explain why price may behave differently around a particular level.
- How is that useful to my trading?
For short-term traders, that makes option expiries a useful addition to the broader picture alongside technical levels, economic data, central bank expectations and headline risk.
EUR/USD
- 1.1075 (EUR 1.13 bn)
- 1.0975 (EUR 1.74 bn)
USD/JPY
- 160.00 (US$ 1.75 bn)
- 159.20 (US$ 1.27 bn)
USD/CAD
- 1.4250 (US$ 1.13 bn)
AUD/USD
- 0.6725 (AUD 448.00 mn)
EUR/GBP
- 0.8360 (EUR 438.99 mn)
What are FX option expiries?
The FX option expiration price levels refer to the strike prices where option contracts are set to expire. These levels include both calls and puts.
When you see "EUR/USD at 1.1600 for €4 billion" it means there is a total of €4 billion worth of options (calls + puts combined) that have a strike price of 1.1600 and are expiring at that specific time (the "New York Cut" at 10:00 AM ET).
Traders watch these levels because they often act as a "magnet" for the price. For example, if there's nothing happening in the market and the price is close to the expiry level, let's say 30-50 pips away, what you will usually see is the price moving into the expiry level. This happens due to the hedging activity of the market makers (banks, dealers and so on).
As the price gets closer to the strike price near expiration, these market makers must aggressively buy or sell the currency to hedge their risk. This hedging activity tends to suppress volatility and keep the price "pinned" close to the strike price until the expiration time passes.

[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: News] What are the main events for today?
The highlights include the US Jobless Claims figures and the first day of Anthropic trading
Reader questions
- Why do jobless claims matter to the market?
Jobless claims provide an early look at the health of the labor market; a significant rise could signal economic weakness and potentially lead to recession fears, depending on the economic context.
- What does it mean for a stock to "start trading on the Nasdaq"?
This means the company, Anthropic in this case, is having its Initial Public Offering or IPO, where its shares become available for the public to buy and sell on the Nasdaq stock exchange for the first time.
- Why do central bank speakers matter?
Remarks from central bank officials can offer clues about future monetary policy, which can significantly impact market sentiment and asset prices.
EUROPEAN SESSION
In the European session, we don't have much on the agenda other than a couple of low-tier releases like the Swiss industrial production and Eurozone current account. The data won't change anything for the respective central banks, so the market reaction will be muted. The focus will remain on the more hawkish Fed and the ongoing US-Iran standoff as they continue to weigh on growth expectations.
AMERICAN SESSION
In the American session, we get the latest US Jobless Claims figures and Anthropic will start trading on the Nasdaq for the first time. Initial Claims are expected at 197K vs 200K prior, while Continuing Claims are seen at 1710K vs 1697K prior. The totality of the US jobs data has been strong for months and we even started to see a pickup in wage growth, which could be signalling a tightening labour market.
The market will likely "ignore" good data since it's widely expected and it's not even the Fed's focus right now. Nevertheless, a deterioration in the next weeks or months could start triggering "recession" fears as rate hikes and potentially more stock market losses will likely weigh on the economy.
Lastly, Anthropic is expected to start trading on the Nasdaq today, under the ticker ANT. There is no confirmed opening time, although regular Nasdaq trading starts at 9:30 ET/14:30 GMT. IPO shares can begin trading later, once the opening auction is completed.

decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: News] investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: Oil holds near $92 as Gulf attacks mount,
Market
moving news for Asian trading on Thursday, November 19, 2026.
Oil held near $92 as Trump weighed new Iran strikes, a tanker was hit in Hormuz and Houthi missile debris hit Riyadh, while gold slipped. AUD sank after a 4.9% jobless print, Ueda kept BOJ hikes in play and Anthropic readied its Nasdaq debut.
The key idea
- Geopolitical events, like tensions in the Gulf region, can significantly impact global commodity prices, especially oil.
- Higher oil prices often lead to inflation fears, which can influence central bank decisions on interest rates.
- Central bank interest rate hikes generally strengthen a currency and can put downward pressure on assets like gold.
Reader questions
- Why did gold prices fall despite increased geopolitical tensions, which often make gold a safe haven? Gold prices fell because the escalating tensions pushed oil higher, increasing inflation fears and strengthening the case for more Fed interest rate hikes. Higher rates typically make non-yielding assets like gold less attractive.
- What is the significance of the Australian unemployment data for the RBA? The jump in Australian unemployment to 4.9% and the significant job losses suggest a weakening labor market. This data makes further interest rate hikes by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) less likely.

decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Commodities] NYT: Trump weighs new Iran strikes as Israel presses for a four- to seven-day air campaign
Trump is weighing a new round of extensive strikes on Iran as Israel presses for a joint four- to seven-day air campaign, officials say. No decision has been made, but the report and a fresh tanker attack in Hormuz have pushed oil prices higher.
The key idea
- Geopolitical tensions, like potential military action in the Middle East, directly impact commodity prices, especially oil.
- A "risk premium" is an extra amount added to a price to account for uncertainty or potential negative events. In this case, it's added to oil prices due to the risk of supply disruptions.
Reader questions
- Why does potential military action in the Middle East affect oil prices so much? Military action in key oil-producing regions or shipping lanes, like the Strait of Hormuz, can disrupt the supply of oil, leading to higher prices.
- What does it mean for oil to be "pricing the risk"? This means that traders are factoring in the possibility of future events, such as military strikes or supply disruptions, into the current price of oil.
- How do higher oil prices impact other markets, like gold and currencies? Higher oil prices can fuel inflation concerns, which may lead central banks to raise interest rates, making non-yielding assets like gold less attractive. Oil-importing countries' currencies, like the yen, can weaken as they need to spend more to buy oil.
A renewed US-Israeli air campaign would raise the risk of Iranian retaliation against Gulf shipping and energy infrastructure. With a loaded tanker already hit in the Strait of Hormuz, traders are likely to keep a larger risk premium in crude until Washington’s intentions are clearer. Higher oil feeds straight into the inflation worries that Fed officials raised this week, adding to the case for further US rate hikes. That’s why gold has tended to weaken rather than rally on escalation in this conflict. Oil importers’ currencies, notably the yen, are vulnerable to a further rise in energy costs. Energy stocks stand to benefit.

BOJ’s Ueda said real rates remain low and financial conditions loose despite past hikes, with strong profits and rising wages helping firms absorb higher costs. He said the Q3 consumption dip was expected and BOJ finances can cope with tightening.
The key idea
- The Bank of Japan (BOJ) is signaling that it is prepared to continue raising interest rates. This is because key economic indicators suggest the Japanese economy can handle higher borrowing costs.
- "Real interest rates" are important here; they represent the interest rate after accounting for inflation. When real rates are low, borrowing is cheaper, which encourages spending and investment.
Reader questions
- Why does the BOJ's financial health matter for its policy decisions? The article mentions that the BOJ's ability to withstand further rate hikes is important. This is because higher rates can affect the central bank's own balance sheet, but Governor Ueda's comments suggest this is not a barrier to tightening policy.
- What does "financial conditions are still loose" mean in this context? It means that despite some rate increases, the overall cost of borrowing and availability of credit in the economy are still relatively easy. This supports economic activity and suggests there is room for the BOJ to tighten further.
These follow-up comments matter more for the path beyond December than for the December decision, which already looked well set. By saying real rates are still low and conditions loose, Ueda leaves room for the 1.75% end-March level many economists expect, and possibly more. That supports higher short-dated JGB yields and gives the yen modest support. The reassurance on BOJ finances and ETF sales removes a technical worry that some had seen as a brake on tightening. Japanese equities may watch the ETF comment closely, since the pace of BOJ selling affects a large holder of the market.

decisions.raw_text:
[INVESTINGLIVE] [Categories: Central Banks] BOJ’s Ueda expects to keep raising rates, warning inflation could overshoot 2% target
BOJ Governor Ueda said the bank expects to keep raising rates as monetary conditions stay accommodative, warning underlying inflation could overshoot the 2% target. He called consumption resilient, backing bets on a December hike to 1.50%.
The key idea
- The Bank of Japan (BOJ) is shifting its focus from fighting deflation to preventing inflation from rising too high.
- This means the BOJ is likely to continue raising interest rates to keep prices stable.
- An "accommodative" monetary policy means the central bank is making it easier and cheaper to borrow money, often to stimulate economic growth.
Reader questions
- What does "overshoot the 2% target" mean for inflation? It means the rate of price increases goes above the central bank's desired level of 2%, which could lead to economic instability.
- Why do Japanese bank stocks benefit from a steeper rate path? A steeper rate path generally means banks can earn more money on the difference between what they pay for deposits and what they earn on loans.
- How does a weak yen impact inflation and the BOJ's actions? A weak yen makes imported goods more expensive, contributing to inflation, and puts pressure on the BOJ to raise rates to strengthen the currency.
Ueda’s remarks firm up the case for a December hike, which should give some support to the yen, although the effect may be limited while the Fed is also raising rates. The emphasis on overshoot risk could matter more for the path beyond December, supporting bets on a move to 1.75% by March and keeping upward pressure on short-dated JGB yields. Japanese bank stocks tend to benefit from a steeper rate path, while exporters lose some of the support from a weak yen. Overnight inflation data will be the next catalyst. A firm print would strengthen expectations for both the December move and the one after it.
---
Earlier:
- BOJ tipped to hike to 1.50% in December, its first three-hike year in 37 years
---
Ueda’s worry is no longer inflation falling short of 2%. It’s inflation overshooting, and with policy still accommodative, that points to more hikes, starting in December.

- BOJ Governor Ueda said the bank expects to keep raising rates because monetary conditions remain accommodative
- He warned of a risk that underlying inflation could overshoot the 2% target

- He described the economy as recovering moderately with some weakness, and consumption as resilient
- A Reuters poll shows 86% of economists expect a hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting

Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Thursday that the central bank expects to keep raising interest rates because monetary conditions remain accommodative, adding that there is a risk underlying inflation could overshoot the BOJ’s 2% target. His remarks, which crossed the wires from 01:03 GMT, reinforce expectations of a December hike and come a day after he said the bank should continue lifting borrowing costs.
Ueda described the economy as recovering moderately, albeit with some weakness, and said consumption has been resilient. He judged underlying inflation to be roughly consistent with the price target, but stressed that the bigger danger now lies on the upside. Anchoring underlying inflation around 2%, he said, is important to stop the risk of an overshoot from materialising.
That framing matters. For years the BOJ’s challenge was getting inflation up to target.
